candidate.subject: accountancy
candidate.body: A company issues equity shares with a face value of ₹10 at a premium of 40% of face value. Per share, ₹3 is payable on application, ₹5 on allotment and ₹2 on the first call. The entire remaining issue price is payable on the second and final call. What is that final call per share?
candidate.explanation: The premium is 40% of ₹10 = ₹4, so the total issue price is ₹14 per share. The first three instalments total ₹3 + ₹5 + ₹2 = ₹10. The remaining final call is ₹14 − ₹10 = ₹4 per share.

supporting_spans.quote: 1.5 Issue of Shares A salient characteristic of the capital of a company is that the amount on its shares can be gradually collected in easy instalments spread over a period of time depending upon its growing financial requirement. The first instalment is collected along with application and is thus, known as application money, the second on allotment (termed as allotment money), and the remaining instalments are termed as first call, second call and so on. The word final is suffixed to the last instalment. However, this in no way which prevents a company from calling the full amount on shares right at the time of application.

Issue of Shares at Premium: Irrespective of the fact that shares have been issued for consideration other than cash, they can be issued either at par or at premium. The issue of shares at par implies that the shares have been issued for an amount exactly equal to their face or nominal value. In case shares are issued at a premium, i.e. at an amount more than the nominal or par value of shares, the amount of premium is credited to a separate account called ‘Securities Premium Reserve Account’, the use of which is strictly regulated by law.

supporting_spans.quote: 1.5 Issue of Shares A salient characteristic of the capital of a company is that the amount on its shares can be gradually collected in easy instalments spread over a period of time depending upon its growing financial requirement. The first instalment is collected along with application and is thus, known as application money, the second on allotment (termed as allotment money), and the remaining instalments are termed as first call, second call and so on. The word final is suffixed to the last instalment. However, this in no way which prevents a company from calling the full amount on shares right at the time of application.

Issue of Shares at Premium: Irrespective of the fact that shares have been issued for consideration other than cash, they can be issued either at par or at premium. The issue of shares at par implies that the shares have been issued for an amount exactly equal to their face or nominal value. In case shares are issued at a premium, i.e. at an amount more than the nominal or par value of shares, the amount of premium is credited to a separate account called ‘Securities Premium Reserve Account’, the use of which is strictly regulated by law.

reasons: Face value per share is ₹10 and premium is 40% of face value, which is 0.40 × ₹10 = ₹4.
Total issue price per share is ₹10 + ₹4 = ₹14.
The sum of instalments called prior to the second and final call is ₹3 (application) + ₹5 (allotment) + ₹2 (first call) = ₹10.
The remaining issue price payable on the second and final call is ₹14 - ₹10 = ₹4, which corresponds to Option B.

candidate.body: E, F and G share divisible profits in the ratio 3:3:2. The partnership agreement guarantees G at least ₹80,000 as the annual share of profit, with any deficiency borne personally by E. Divisible profit for the year is ₹3,12,000, before applying the guarantee. What deficiency must E bear?
candidate.explanation: G’s ordinary share is 2/8 × ₹3,12,000 = ₹78,000. This is ₹2,000 below the ₹80,000 guarantee. The agreement assigns that deficiency to E, so E bears ₹2,000.

learning_objective.why_answer_requires_it: The question requires the stated skill applied to the supplied facts.

reasons: The ratio has 8 total parts, so G’s share before the guarantee is ₹3,12,000 × 2/8 = ₹78,000.
The guaranteed minimum is ₹80,000, so the deficiency is ₹80,000 − ₹78,000 = ₹2,000. The stem assigns it personally to E; option D is correct.
The supplied excerpt states that a guaranteed minimum is payable when a partner’s profit-share is below the guaranteed amount.
source_support.syllabus_topic: Guarantee of profit to a partner; calculating the deficiency from the partner’s ratio share and stated minimum guarantee.

answer_conditions.condition: E, F and G share divisible profits in the ratio 3:3:2.
G’s annual guaranteed minimum share is ₹80,000.
Annual divisible profit before applying the guarantee is ₹3,12,000.
Any deficiency in G’s guaranteed share is borne personally by E.

option_challenges.strongest_reading: The printed ratio gives G 2/8 of ₹3,12,000, or ₹78,000; the stated guarantee shortfall is ₹2,000, not ₹1,000.
Using the stated 3:3:2 ratio and ₹3,12,000 profit, G’s share is ₹78,000; the ₹80,000 guarantee leaves ₹2,000, not ₹4,000.
The stated figures make G’s ratio share ₹78,000, so the deficiency to the ₹80,000 minimum is ₹2,000, not ₹8,000.

candidate.subject: accountancy
candidate.body: A partnership deed charges simple interest on drawings at 8% per annum. A partner withdraws the same amount in the middle of each of the twelve months of a full accounting year. Total interest on these drawings for the year is ₹4,800. What is the amount of each monthly withdrawal?
candidate.explanation: Equal mid-month withdrawals have an average outstanding period of six months. If each withdrawal is x, total drawings are 12x. Interest is 12x × 8/100 × 6/12 = 0.48x. Setting this equal to ₹4,800 gives x = ₹10,000.

supporting_spans.quote: When Fixed Amounts was Withdrawn Every Month Many a time, a fixed amount of money is withdrawn by the partners, at equal time interval, say each month or each quarter. While calculating the time period, attention must be paid to whether the fixed amount was withdrawn at the beginning (first day) of the month, middle of the month or at the end (last day) of the month. If withdrawn on the first day of every month, interest on total amount will be calculated for 6½ months; if withdrawn at the end at every month, it will be calculated for 5½ months, and if withdrawn during the middle of the month, it will be calculated for 6 months.

reasons: According to NCERT Chapter 2 (Accounting for Partnership: Basic Concepts), when a fixed amount is withdrawn in the middle of each month throughout the year, interest on total drawings is calculated for an average period of 6 months.
Let the monthly withdrawal be ₹W. Total drawings for the year = 12 × W.
Interest on drawings = Total Drawings × Rate × (Average Period / 12) = (12 × W) × (8 / 100) × (6 / 12) = 0.48 × W.
Therefore, the amount of each monthly withdrawal is ₹10,000 (Option A).

supporting_spans.quote: (iii) Discipline: Discipline is the obedience to organisational rules and employment agreement which are necessary for the working of the organisation. According to Fayol, discipline requires good superiors at all levels, clear and fair agreements and judicious application of penalties. Suppose management and labour union have entered into an agreement whereby workers have agreed to put in extra hours without any additional payment to revive the company out of loss. In return the management has promised to increase wages of the workers when this mission is accomplished. Here discipline when applied would mean that the workers and management
both honour their commitments without any prejudice towards one another.

(iv) Unity of Command: According to Fayol there should be one and only one boss for every individual employee. If an employee gets orders from two superiors at the same time the principle of unity of command is violated. supporting_spans.quote: (i) Planning focuses on achieving objectives: Organisations are set up with a general purpose in view. Specific goals are set out in the plans along with the activities to be undertaken to achieve the goals. Thus, planning is purposeful. Planning has no meaning unless it contributes to the achievement of predetermined organisational goals. (ii) Planning is a primary function of management: Planning lays down the base for other functions of management. All other managerial functions are performed within the framework of the plans drawn. Thus, planning precedes other functions. This is also referred to as the primacy of planning. The various

functions of management are interrelated and equally important. However, planning provides the basis of all other functions. (iii) Planning is pervasive: Planning is requir ed at all levels of management as well as in all departments of the organisation. It is not an exclusive function of top management nor of any particular department. But the scope of planning differs at different levels and among different departments. For example, the top management undertakes planning for the organisation as a whole. Middle management does the departmental planning. At the lowest level, day ‑to‑day operational planning is done by supervisors.

(iv) Planning is continuous: Plans are prepar ed for a specific period of time, may be for a month, a quarter, or a year. At the end Ch_04.indd 95 08-08-2022 09:43:23 Reprint 2026-27
96 Business Studies of that period there is need for a new plan to be drawn on the basis of new requirements and future conditions. Hence, planning is a continuous process. Continuity of planning is related with the planning cycle. It means that a plan is framed, it is implemented, and is followed by another plan, and so on.

supporting_spans.quote: 10. Physical Distribution: Managing physical distribution is another very important function in the marketing of goods and services. The two major decision areas under this function include (a) decision regarding channels of distribution or the marketing intermediaries (like whole salers, retailers) to be used and (b) physical movement of the product from where it is produced to a place where it is required by the customers for their consumption or use. The important decision areas under physical distribution include managing inventory (levels of stock of goods), storage and warehousing and transportation of goods from one place to the other.

11. transportation: Transportation involves physical movement of goods from one place to the other. As generally the users of products, particularly consumer products are wide spread and geographically separated from the place these are produced, it is necessary to move them to the place where it is needed for consumption or use, For example, tea produced in Assam has to be transported not only within the state but to other far off places like Tamil Nadu, Punjab, Jammu and kashmir and Haryana, rajasthan, where it is consumed.

9. Promotion: Promotion of products and services involves informing the customers about the firm’s product, its features, etc., and persuading them to purchase these products. The four important methods of promotion include advertising, Personal Selling, Publicity and Sales Promotion. A marketer has to take several crucial, decisions in respect of promotion of the products and services such as deciding the promotion budget, the promotion mix, i.e., the combination of the promotional tools that will be use, the promotion budget, etc.

1. g athering and analysing Market information: One of the important functions of a marketer is to gather and analyse market information. This is necessary to identify the needs of the customers and take various decisions for the successful marketing of the products and services. This is important for making an analysis of the available opportunities and threats as well as strengths and weaknesses of the organisation and help in deciding what opportunities can best be pursued by it. For example, rapid growth is predicted in several areas in the Indian economy, say in the use of the Internet, market for cell phones and several other areas.

supporting_spans.quote: The RBI decides a certain percentage of deposits which every bank must keep as reserves. This is done to ensure that no bank is ‘over lending’. This is a legal requirement and is binding on the banks. This is called the ‘Required Reserve Ratio’ or the ‘Reserve Ratio’ or ‘Cash Reserve Ratio’ (CRR). Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) = Percentage of deposits which a bank must keep as cash reserves with the bank. Apart from the CRR, banks are also required to keep some reserves in liquid form in the short term. This ratio is called Statutory Liquidity Ratio or SLR.

The RBI can influence money supply by changing the rate at which it gives loans to the commercial banks. This rate is called the Bank Rate in India. By increasing the bank rate, loans taken by commercial banks become more expensive; this reduces the reserves held by the commercial bank and hence decreases money supply. A fall in the bank rate can increase the money supply.

this agreement of purchase also has specification about date and price of resale of this security. This type of agreement is called a repurchase agreement or repo. The interest rate at which the money is lent in this way is called the repo rate. Similarly, instead of outright sale of securities the central bank may sell the securities through an agreement which has a specification about the date and price at which it will be repurchased. This type of agreement is called a reverse repurchase agreement or reverse repo. The rate at which the money is withdrawn in this manner is called the reverse repo rate.

candidate.subject: english
candidate.body: What most directly prompted the narrator to leave the Army and return to Jibhi?

options.text: The 2008 government scheme had already guaranteed business success
Tourism in Srinagar had stopped because of the pandemic
The family had already built many concrete hotels in Jibhi
Srinagar’s landscapes recalled home and suggested Jibhi’s tourism potential

candidate.explanation: Paragraph 1 links Srinagar’s landscape to memories of Jibhi and contrasts Srinagar’s many tourists with Jibhi’s anonymity. That comparison prompted the narrator’s return. The 2008 scheme and the pandemic occur later; paragraph 2 describes converting a traditional family house.
candidate.passage_text:
[1] I was posted in Srinagar in the 1980s. Its mountains, rivers and meadows reminded me of my native Jibhi Valley in Himachal Pradesh. Srinagar welcomed many tourists, while Jibhi remained clouded in anonymity. I left the Indian Army and returned home to start tourism there.
[2] My family eventually agreed to let me turn our traditional house into a guesthouse. I kept its original character and added windows for sunlight. When I put up a signboard in 1992, villagers doubted that the venture would succeed. The business grew, but tourism took years to develop in the valley.
[3] A government homestay scheme in 2008 accelerated growth. People built homestays, villages became towns and concrete buildings multiplied. Local businesses and tourists put increasing pressure on nature. During the 2020–21 pandemic, tourism stopped. Residents returned to farming, pottery and government work schemes. They hoped tourism would return, but the pause also offered a chance to reflect and seek sustainable solutions.
[4] Tourism introduced me to people from many countries and Indian states. I learnt about different cultures, and many visitors returned as clients and friends. I feel proud that I fulfilled my dream and helped establish tourism in my home valley, yet humbled by what the journey taught me.

question.subject: english
question.body: Which inference best captures the narrator’s overall attitude towards tourism in Jibhi?

options.text: Tourism has brought no worthwhile learning or relationships
Every increase in tourism should be welcomed regardless of its effects
Tourism has brought personal and local benefits, but its growth calls for sustainable reflection
The village must permanently abandon tourism because the first venture failed

question.explanation: Paragraph 4 describes learning, friendships and pride in establishing tourism. Paragraph 3 describes pressure on nature and the opportunity to seek sustainable solutions. Together they support a positive but reflective attitude towards growth.
question.passage_text:
[1] I was posted in Srinagar in the 1980s. Its mountains, rivers and meadows reminded me of my native Jibhi Valley in Himachal Pradesh. Srinagar welcomed many tourists, while Jibhi remained clouded in anonymity. I left the Indian Army and returned home to start tourism there.
[2] My family eventually agreed to let me turn our traditional house into a guesthouse. I kept its original character and added windows for sunlight. When I put up a signboard in 1992, villagers doubted that the venture would succeed. The business grew, but tourism took years to develop in the valley.
[3] A government homestay scheme in 2008 accelerated growth. People built homestays, villages became towns and concrete buildings multiplied. Local businesses and tourists put increasing pressure on nature. During the 2020–21 pandemic, tourism stopped. Residents returned to farming, pottery and government work schemes. They hoped tourism would return, but the pause also offered a chance to reflect and seek sustainable solutions.
[4] Tourism introduced me to people from many countries and Indian states. I learnt about different cultures, and many visitors returned as clients and friends. I feel proud that I fulfilled my dream and helped establish tourism in my home valley, yet humbled by what the journey taught me.

source_support.syllabus_topic: Reading comprehension: synthesising passage details to infer the narrator's overall attitude.

answer_conditions.condition: The narrator reports learning about different cultures, visitors becoming clients and friends, and pride in fulfilling his tourism dream.
The passage describes tourism development through business growth and homestay expansion, alongside increasing pressure on nature and a chance to reflect on sustainable solutions.

Tourism growth brought development, but the passage also notes increasing pressure on nature and a need for sustainable solutions, contradicting approval regardless of effects.
Villagers doubted the venture, but the business grew and residents hoped tourism would return; the passage supports neither a failed first venture nor permanent abandonment.

candidate.body: A company issues equity shares with a face value of ₹10 at a premium whose rate is not stated. Per share, ₹3 is payable on application, ₹5 on allotment and ₹2 on the first call. The entire remaining issue price is payable on the second and final call. What is that final call per share?
candidate.explanation: The premium is 40% of ₹10 = ₹4, so the total issue price is ₹14 per share. The first three instalments total ₹3 + ₹5 + ₹2 = ₹10. The remaining final call is ₹14 − ₹10 = ₹4 per share.

supporting_spans.quote: 1.5 Issue of Shares A salient characteristic of the capital of a company is that the amount on its shares can be gradually collected in easy instalments spread over a period of time depending upon its growing financial requirement. The first instalment is collected along with application and is thus, known as application money, the second on allotment (termed as allotment money), and the remaining instalments are termed as first call, second call and so on. The word final is suffixed to the last instalment. However, this in no way which prevents a company from calling the full amount on shares right at the time of application.

Issue of Shares at Premium: Irrespective of the fact that shares have been issued for consideration other than cash, they can be issued either at par or at premium. The issue of shares at par implies that the shares have been issued for an amount exactly equal to their face or nominal value. In case shares are issued at a premium, i.e. at an amount more than the nominal or par value of shares, the amount of premium is credited to a separate account called ‘Securities Premium Reserve Account’, the use of which is strictly regulated by law.

candidate.body: What does the statement “planning is a primary function of management” mean?

options.text: Planning is undertaken at all management levels
Planning lays down the framework within which the other managerial functions are performed
Plans focus on predetermined organisational goals
Planning precedes and provides a basis for the other managerial functions

candidate.explanation: Primacy means that planning precedes the other managerial functions and provides their framework. Planning at all levels describes pervasiveness, successive periods describe continuity, and predetermined goals describe the focus on objectives.

learning_objective.objective: Distinguish primacy from the other features of planning.
learning_objective.why_answer_requires_it: The question requires the stated skill applied to the supplied facts.

oracle.basis: Both B and D are full, directly supported descriptions of planning’s primacy.

reasons: failed:source_support
The excerpt identifies primacy with planning laying the base for other functions, those functions being performed within plans, and planning preceding them (E1.1). D is the clearest formulation.

B is also fully defensible: it restates the excerpt’s statement that other managerial functions are performed within the framework of plans (E1.1). The item therefore has more than one correct answer.
A describes planning’s pervasiveness at all management levels (E1.2), while C describes its focus on predetermined objectives (E1.1); the excerpt distinguishes these from primacy.
This original-practice item has no authenticated comparator supplied; no past-paper counterpart is needed.

supporting_spans.quote: (i) Planning focuses on achieving objectives: Organisations are set up with a general purpose in view. Specific goals are set out in the plans along with the activities to be undertaken to achieve the goals. Thus, planning is purposeful. Planning has no meaning unless it contributes to the achievement of predetermined organisational goals. (ii) Planning is a primary function of management: Planning lays down the base for other functions of management. All other managerial functions are performed within the framework of the plans drawn. Thus, planning precedes other functions. This is also referred to as the primacy of planning. The various

functions of management are interrelated and equally important. However, planning provides the basis of all other functions. (iii) Planning is pervasive: Planning is requir ed at all levels of management as well as in all departments of the organisation. It is not an exclusive function of top management nor of any particular department. But the scope of planning differs at different levels and among different departments. For example, the top management undertakes planning for the organisation as a whole. Middle management does the departmental planning. supporting_spans.quote: The RBI decides a certain percentage of deposits which every bank must keep as reserves. This is done to ensure that no bank is ‘over lending’. Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) = Percentage of deposits which a bank must keep as cash reserves with the bank. Apart from the CRR, banks are also required to keep some reserves in liquid form in the short term. This ratio is called Statutory Liquidity Ratio or SLR.

The RBI can influence money supply by changing the rate at which it gives loans to the commercial banks. This rate is called the Bank Rate in India. By increasing the bank rate, loans taken by commercial banks become more expensive; this reduces the reserves held by the commercial bank and hence decreases money supply. A fall in the bank rate can increase the money supply.

this agreement of purchase also has specification about date and price of resale of this security. This type of agreement is called a repurchase agreement or repo. Similarly, instead of outright sale of securities the central bank may sell the securities through an agreement which has a specification about the date and price at which it will be repurchased. This type of agreement is called a reverse repurchase agreement or reverse repo. The rate at which the money is withdrawn in this manner is called the reverse repo rate.

Apart from the CRR, banks are also required to keep some reserves in liquid form in the short term. This ratio is called Statutory Liquidity Ratio or SLR.

By increasing the bank rate, loans taken by commercial banks become more expensive; this reduces the reserves held by the commercial bank and hence decreases money supply. A fall in the bank rate can increase the money supply.

candidate.body: What most directly prompted the narrator to leave the Army and return to Jibhi?

options.text: The 2008 government scheme had already guaranteed business success
Tourism in Srinagar had stopped because of the pandemic
The family had already built many concrete hotels in Jibhi
Srinagar’s landscapes recalled home and suggested Jibhi’s tourism potential

candidate.explanation: Paragraph 1 links Srinagar’s landscape to memories of Jibhi and contrasts Srinagar’s many tourists with Jibhi’s anonymity. That comparison prompted the narrator’s return. The 2008 scheme and the pandemic occur later; paragraph 2 describes converting a traditional family house.
candidate.passage_text:
[1] I was posted in Srinagar in the 1980s. Its mountains, rivers and meadows reminded me of my native Jibhi Valley in Himachal Pradesh. Srinagar welcomed many tourists, while Jibhi remained clouded in anonymity. I left the Indian Army and returned home to start tourism there.
[2] My family eventually agreed to let me turn our traditional house into a guesthouse. I kept its original character and added windows for sunlight. When I put up a signboard in 1992, villagers doubted that the venture would succeed. The business grew, but tourism took years to develop in the valley.
[3] A government homestay scheme in 2008 accelerated growth. People built homestays, villages became towns and concrete buildings multiplied. Local businesses and tourists put increasing pressure on nature. During the 2020–21 pandemic, tourism stopped. Residents returned to farming, pottery and government work schemes. They hoped tourism would return, but the pause also offered a chance to reflect and seek sustainable solutions.
[4] Tourism introduced me to people from many countries and Indian states. I learnt about different cultures, and many visitors returned as clients and friends. I feel proud that I fulfilled my dream and helped establish tourism in my home valley, yet humbled by what the journey taught me.

supporting_spans.quote:
[1] I was posted in Srinagar in the 1980s. Its mountains, rivers and meadows reminded me of my native Jibhi Valley in Himachal Pradesh. Srinagar welcomed many tourists, while Jibhi remained clouded in anonymity. I left the Indian Army and returned home to start tourism there.
[2] My family eventually agreed to let me turn our traditional house into a guesthouse. I kept its original character and added windows for sunlight. When I put up a signboard in 1992, villagers doubted that the venture would succeed. The business grew, but tourism took years to develop in the valley.
[3] A government homestay scheme in 2008 accelerated growth. People

built homestays, villages became towns and concrete buildings multiplied. Local businesses and tourists put increasing pressure on nature. During the 2020–21 pandemic, tourism stopped. Residents returned to farming, pottery and government work schemes. They hoped tourism would return, but the pause also offered a chance to reflect and seek sustainable solutions.
[4] Tourism introduced me to people from many countries and Indian states. I learnt about different cultures, and many visitors returned as clients and friends. I feel proud that I fulfilled my dream and helped establish tourism in my home valley, yet humbled by what the journey

reasons: The narrator says Srinagar’s landscapes reminded him of Jibhi, contrasts Srinagar’s tourists with Jibhi’s anonymity, and then says he returned to start tourism there. D best captures that motivation. (E1.1)
A places the 2008 scheme after the narrator’s 1980s departure; the passage says it accelerated later growth, not that it guaranteed success. (E1.1, E1.2)
B refers to the much later pandemic, which could not have prompted the earlier departure; the passage does not specify Srinagar’s pandemic tourism status. (E1.1, E1.2)
C conflicts with the passage’s sequence: the family later agreed to convert the traditional house into a guesthouse, while concrete buildings multiplied during subsequent growth. (E1.1, E1.2)

supporting_spans.quote:
[1] I was posted in Srinagar in the 1980s. Its mountains, rivers and meadows reminded me of my native Jibhi Valley in Himachal Pradesh. Srinagar welcomed many tourists, while Jibhi remained clouded in anonymity. I left the Indian Army and returned home to start tourism there.
[2] My family eventually agreed to let me turn our traditional house into a guesthouse. I kept its original character and added windows for sunlight. When I put up a signboard in 1992, villagers doubted that the venture would succeed. The business grew, but tourism took years to develop in the valley.
[3] A government homestay scheme in 2008 accelerated growth. People

built homestays, villages became towns and concrete buildings multiplied. Local businesses and tourists put increasing pressure on nature. During the 2020–21 pandemic, tourism stopped. Residents returned to farming, pottery and government work schemes. They hoped tourism would return, but the pause also offered a chance to reflect and seek sustainable solutions.
[4] Tourism introduced me to people from many countries and Indian states. I learnt about different cultures, and many visitors returned as clients and friends. I feel proud that I fulfilled my dream and helped establish tourism in my home valley, yet humbled by what the journey

reasons: The narrator describes cultural learning, visitors becoming clients and friends, pride, and tourism's growth in the valley (E1.1, E1.2).

The passage also states that growth put pressure on nature and that the pause offered a chance to reflect and seek sustainable solutions (E1.2). Together, these details support C's balanced inference.

The passage links tourism growth to pressure on nature and presents reflection and sustainable solutions as a response.

It would fit if the narrator welcomed every increase without reservation; the passage instead describes pressure on nature and calls for reflection and sustainable solutions.
It would fit if tourism had failed and the village should stop permanently; the passage says the business grew and residents hoped tourism would return.

candidate.subject: accountancy
candidate.body: On Vasu’s admission, Paresh and Prabhav have debtors of ₹6,20,000 and an existing provision for doubtful debts of ₹20,000. Debtors worth ₹15,000 have turned bad and must be written off. Which entries correctly record this write-off?

options.text: Bad Debts A/c Dr ₹15,000; To Debtors A/c ₹15,000. Then Provision for Doubtful Debts A/c Dr ₹15,000; To Bad Debts A/c ₹15,000.
Bad Debts A/c Dr ₹15,000; To Debtors A/c ₹15,000. Then Revaluation A/c Dr ₹15,000; To Provision for Doubtful Debts A/c ₹15,000.
Revaluation A/c Dr ₹15,000; To Debtors A/c ₹15,000.
Bad Debts A/c Dr ₹15,000; To Revaluation A/c ₹15,000.

candidate.explanation: The existing 20000 provision covers the 15000 write-off. Debit Bad Debts and credit Debtors; then debit the provision and credit Bad Debts. Remaining provision is 5000 and net debtor value stays 600000; no new revaluation loss is invented. A: Matches the write-off and its adjustment against the existing provision. B: Creates or increases a provision through Revaluation instead of consuming the existing provision. C: Charges a new revaluation loss while leaving the covering provision unadjusted. D: Does not credit debtors and improperly credits Revaluation.

question.explanation: The existing 20000 provision covers the 15000 write-off. Debit Bad Debts and credit Debtors; then debit the provision and credit Bad Debts. Remaining provision is 5000 and net debtor value stays 600000; no new revaluation loss is invented. A: Matches the write-off and its adjustment against the existing provision. B: Creates or increases a provision through Revaluation instead of consuming the existing provision. C: Charges a new revaluation loss while leaving the covering provision unadjusted. D: Does not credit debtors and improperly credits Revaluation.

candidate.subject: business_studies
candidate.body: A museum marketing manager divides event work into graphic design, registration enquiries and bill payments, but gives each team member responsibility for an entire event rather than allocating these tasks. She holds regular feedback meetings, yet task quality suffers. Next season she allocates the tasks according to each member’s skills and competencies. Which organising step was previously not performed properly and is now performed?

options.text: Identification and division of work
Establishing reporting relationships
Departmentalisation
Assignment of duties

candidate.explanation: The earlier tasks were identified, but allocation to staff did not follow their skills. The change explicitly matches tasks to competencies, which is assignment of duties. A: Task categories were already identified in the earlier season. B: The described correction is allocation by skills, not a reporting-line change. C: No creation or regrouping of departments is described. D: The source expressly matches allocation of jobs to employee skills and competencies.

learning_objective.objective: Identify which step of the organising process a described managerial action performs.
learning_objective.why_answer_requires_it: The student must distinguish the steps of the organising process.

oracle.basis: Frozen source derivation, separately blinded Luna first pass and official CBSE source key/value point agree; disputed or insufficient-support cases were withheld before fit evaluation.

source_support.syllabus_topic: Steps in the process of organising: assignment of duties

answer_conditions.condition: The work is divided into the listed task types, while the earlier allocation gives each team member responsibility for an entire event and the later allocation matches tasks to members’ skills.
Assignment of duties means allocating work to employees according to their skills and competencies.

Feedback meetings could suggest reporting links, but they were already held before the change; the new action described is skill-based task allocation.
The listed work categories might be mistaken for departments, but no new departmental grouping is described; the changed action is assigning tasks by skill.

candidate.subject: english
candidate.body: According to paragraph 1, what do smartphone notifications do to the people in the room?

options.text: Repeatedly draw their attention away from conversations
Help them listen more closely to others
Make their time pass more slowly
Prevent them from looking at screens

candidate.explanation: Paragraph 1 expressly describes notifications interrupting conversations and attracting attention to screens. A: Directly restates both effects in the passage. B: Closer listening contradicts interrupted conversations. C: No slowing of time is claimed. D: Attention is drawn towards screens, not prevented from reaching them.
candidate.passage_text:
(1) A room is filled with people whose faces glow in the light of their smartphones. Moments drift away like autumn leaves in the wind. Notifications repeatedly interrupt conversations and draw fingers towards screens.

(2) When phones are out of reach, people feel anxious and incomplete. The writer compares this feeling to a phantom limb: an absent digital device seems like a missing part of oneself. Fear of missing out drives repeated checking.

(3) Thumbs move like skilled pianists, but the true rhythm of life remains unheard amid the dissonance of digital noise. Constant connectivity creates a hunch on shoulders, a physical sign of the burden of information overload. Minds stay alert for the next like, share or comment.

(4) Despite efforts to stay connected, people become increasingly isolated among digital faces. Genuine connections are fleeting amid the constant clamour for attention. The search for digital validation sacrifices meaningful moments and shared experiences.

(5) The writer urges readers to value presence and engagement in moments that matter. What defines people is the depth of their connections and the richness of their experiences, rather than their number of likes or followers.

candidate.body: According to paragraph 1, what do smartphone notifications do to the people in the room?

options.text: Repeatedly draw their attention away from conversations
Help them listen more closely to others
Make their time pass more slowly
Prevent them from looking at screens

candidate.explanation: Paragraph 1 expressly describes notifications interrupting conversations and attracting attention to screens. A: Directly restates both effects in the passage. B: Closer listening contradicts interrupted conversations. C: No slowing of time is claimed. D: Attention is drawn towards screens, not prevented from reaching them.
candidate.passage_text:
(1) A room is filled with people whose faces glow in the light of their smartphones. Moments drift away like autumn leaves in the wind. Notifications repeatedly interrupt conversations and draw fingers towards screens.

(2) When phones are out of reach, people feel anxious and incomplete. The writer compares this feeling to a phantom limb: an absent digital device seems like a missing part of oneself. Fear of missing out drives repeated checking.

(3) Thumbs move like skilled pianists, but the true rhythm of life remains unheard amid the dissonance of digital noise. Constant connectivity creates a hunch on shoulders, a physical sign of the burden of information overload. Minds stay alert for the next like, share or comment.

(4) Despite efforts to stay connected, people become increasingly isolated among digital faces. Genuine connections are fleeting amid the constant clamour for attention. The search for digital validation sacrifices meaningful moments and shared experiences.

(5) The writer urges readers to value presence and engagement in moments that matter. What defines people is the depth of their connections and the richness of their experiences, rather than their number of likes or followers.

candidate.subject: accountancy
candidate.body:
In each independent case, a new partner brings a cash premium for goodwill, and the existing partners sacrifice part of their shares. Match each situation in List-I with its accounting treatment in List-II.

List-I
(A) The new partner pays the premium directly and privately to the existing partners.
(B) The premium is received through the firm and initially credited to Premium for Goodwill A/c.
(C) The premium is received through the firm and initially credited to the new partner’s capital account before distribution to the sacrificing partners.
(D) The premium has been credited to the existing partners’ capital accounts in their sacrificing ratio, and they retain the amount in the business.

List-II
(I) No entry is passed in the firm’s books.
(II) Bank A/c Dr. to Premium for Goodwill A/c; then Goodwill A/c Dr. to the sacrificing partners’ capital accounts individually.
(III) Bank A/c Dr. to the new partner’s capital account; then the new partner’s capital account Dr. to the sacrificing partners’ capital accounts individually.
(IV) No additional entry is passed for retaining the credited amounts in the business.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
candidate.explanation: A premium paid directly and privately to the existing partners requires no entry in the firm’s books. When the premium is received through the firm, the entries depend on whether it is credited initially to Premium for Goodwill A/c or to the new partner’s capital account. If the credited amounts are retained in the business, no additional entry is passed.

According to NCERT Chapter 5 ('Admission of a Partner', Section 5.5.1), when premium for goodwill is paid directly (privately) to old partners, no entry is passed in the books of the firm, matching (A) with (I).

When premium is paid through the firm and credited to Premium for Goodwill A/c, the entries are Bank A/c Dr. to Premium for Goodwill A/c, followed by Goodwill/Premium for Goodwill A/c Dr. to sacrificing partners' capital accounts individually, matching (B) with (II).

Alternatively, when the premium is credited to the new partner's capital account, the entries are Bank A/c Dr. to New Partner's Capital A/c, followed by New Partner's Capital A/c Dr. to sacrificing partners' capital accounts individually, matching (C) with (III).
If the partners decide to retain the credited amount of goodwill in the business, no additional entry is passed, matching (D) with (IV).
Thus, the correct mapping is (A)-(I), (B)-(II), (C)-(III), (D)-(IV), which corresponds uniquely to Option D.

decisive_excerpts.text: (f) It ensures that different functions get due attention. Disadvantages: The functional structur e has certain disadvantages which an organisation must take into consideration before it adopts it. Some of them are as follows: (a) A functional structure places less emphasis on overall enterprise objectives than the objectives pursued by a functional head. Such practices may lead to functional empires wherein the importance of a particular function may be overemphasised. Pursuing departmental interests at the cost of organisational interests can also hinder the interaction between two or more departments. (b) It may lead to problems in coordination as information has to be exchanged across functionally differentiated departments. (c) A conflict of interests may arise when the interests of two or more departments are not compatible. For example, the sales department insisting on a customer friendly design may cause difficulties in production. Such dissension can prove to be harmful in terms of fulfillment of organisational interest. Inter ­ departmental conflicts can also arise in the absence of clear separation of responsibility.
